content.title: Can a reasonable person believe in miracles?
content.summary: God acts in his world; not every remarkable report is true.

answer.text: Yes. The Creator is not imprisoned by the ordinary patterns of his creation. Christianity depends on God's supernatural acts, supremely Christ's resurrection. That conviction does not require us to accept every claim of a miracle: Scripture itself commands discernment.

reasoning.text: God both sustains ordinary events and is free to act beyond ordinary means.
The resurrection is essential to the gospel, not an optional embellishment.
An impressive sign is not sufficient grounds for receiving false teaching.

conclusion.text: We should confess the miracles God reveals and test additional reports without confusing wonder with truth.

sections.text: John records signs so that readers may believe Jesus is the Christ. Their meaning concerns his identity, not merely the occurrence of something unusual. Read what the author says the sign demonstrates.
sections.title: Read the event in its setting

sections.text: Ask what occurred, what the witnesses claim and whether an explanation goes beyond their testimony. Those are practical applications of testing claims. A sincere or moving story should not be treated as automatically reliable.
sections.title: Discernment belongs to faith

sections.text: Hume's essay has two parts, and the second is often forgotten. Even granting that testimony might in principle establish a miracle, he argued, no actual report has ever done so. He gave four reasons: no miracle has been attested by enough witnesses of good sense, education and integrity, in a public place where fraud would be exposed; people love to tell and believe wonders; miracle stories abound chiefly among “ignorant and barbarous nations”; and the miracles of rival religions cancel each other out, since each is offered to prove a different faith. This is the stronger half of his case, because it asks about evidence rather than definitions. It deserves an answer in its own terms, which the article on Hume gives at length.
sections.title: Hume's second argument: the actual reports

sections.text: George Campbell, a Scottish minister, answered Hume in 1762: our trust in testimony is itself learned from experience, so experience cannot be uniform against a miracle unless every report has been ruled out in advance. William Paley in 1794 asked his readers to imagine twelve men of known honesty who chose to suffer rather than retract their account of a miracle they had seen, and whether Hume's maxim really obliges us to disbelieve them. The Baptist apologist E. Y. Mullins in 1905 added that if testimony could never establish what runs against past experience, nothing happening for the first time could ever be proved. In 2000 the philosopher of science John Earman, writing as no believer, argued from probability theory that Hume's argument is largely a failure, though he did not conclude that any miracle occurred. None of these replies shows that a given miracle happened. They show that the question cannot be closed before the evidence is heard.
sections.title: How Christians and philosophers have replied

sections.text: On this, the sources agree more than one might expect. Peter tells a Jerusalem crowd that Jesus was attested by miracles “as you yourselves know”. Jesus' opponents did not deny his deeds; they said he cast out demons by the prince of demons. Josephus calls him “a doer of wonderful works”. The pagan critic Celsus, writing about 175, said Jesus learned magic in Egypt. Hostile witnesses explaining the deeds away are evidence that the deeds were reported from the start. The Gospels are also restrained: Jesus refuses to perform signs on demand, and in Nazareth he did few mighty works because of their unbelief. The miracles point to who he is, and the greatest sign he offered was his own resurrection.
sections.title: Did Jesus do deeds people called miracles?

sections.text: Reports of healings and other wonders come today from every continent; the New Testament scholar Craig Keener gathered hundreds of them in 2011, many with medical documentation, to argue that eyewitness claims of miracles are common and not confined to the credulous. Christians agree that God still answers prayer and may heal. Southern Baptists differ on a narrower question: whether the miraculous gifts of 1 Corinthians 12, such as healing, tongues and prophecy, continue as they were given to the apostolic church. Some hold that those gifts confirmed the apostles' message and ceased with them, pointing to Hebrews 2:3-4. Others hold that they continue, pointing to 1 Corinthians 12–14 and to the lack of any text that says they end before Christ returns. The Baptist Faith and Message does not settle this, so the site does not choose. Both sides agree that every claim is tested by Scripture.
sections.title: Miracles today, and the gifts question

content.objection: A miracle contradicts the regularity of nature.

reply.text: That is not quite Hume's argument. In section 10 of his Enquiry (1748), David Hume argued that a wise person proportions belief to the evidence; that the laws of nature rest on firm and unalterable experience, the strongest proof we have; and that no testimony can establish a miracle unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event it reports. He then argued that no actual report has ever met that test. George Campbell replied in 1762 that the argument assumes its conclusion: experience counts as uniform only if every report of a miracle has been set aside beforehand, and testimony is itself one of our ordinary sources of knowledge, often rightly believed against what we expected. Regularity describes God's ordinary ordering of the world; it does not establish his inability to act exceptionally. The historical question about a particular event still deserves careful examination.

heldBy: David Hume (Enquiry, 1748, section X, part II)
objections.objection: Every religion has its miracle stories, and each is offered to prove that religion true. Since they cannot all be true, they discredit one another: the miracles of Rome, of ancient Arabia and of China destroy each other's testimony, and the Christian ones go down with the rest.

reply.text: The argument assumes every report is equally attested. It is not. Christianity's central claim is a single public event, reported within a few years by named witnesses, some hostile beforehand, who stood to gain nothing. Many other reports are late, anonymous or tied to no checkable event. Scripture itself warns that false signs exist; the Egyptian magicians copied some of Moses' signs. So the existence of false miracle claims calls for testing each claim, which is what the Bible commands, not for rejecting all of them unheard.

heldBy: David Friedrich Strauss (Life of Jesus, 1835; Eliot's translation 1846)
objections.objection: The absolute cause never breaks into the chain of finite causes by single acts of intervention. Any account in which God acts directly, or a person works a miracle, is to that extent not history but myth, the product of a community's faith.

reply.text: This is a philosophical starting point, not a finding. Strauss lays it down as his first test before examining any text, so the conclusion is fixed before the evidence is read. If the God who made and sustains the world exists, there is nothing irrational in his acting in it for a purpose; Scripture describes the ordinary order as his faithfulness, not as a barrier to him. Whether he has acted on a given occasion is then a question of evidence, which is where the argument should be had.

citations.locator: Introduction, §16, p. 71 (1860 printing of Eliot's translation)

heldBy: Bart D. Ehrman (debate with W. L. Craig, 2006; How Jesus Became God, 2014)
objections.objection: Historians can only say what probably happened, and by definition a miracle is the least probable event there is. So even if a miracle happened, a historian as historian could never conclude that it did; any natural explanation, however unlikely, is more probable.

reply.text: Probability depends on what else we know. If there is no God, a resurrection is wildly improbable; if God exists and Jesus' life gives reason to expect him to act, it is not. Historians routinely conclude that unusual events occurred when the evidence is strong. Ehrman's rule would forbid concluding a miracle even if it had happened, which turns a method into a verdict. The question is weighed at length in the case study of the Craig–Ehrman debate.

limit.text: An unexplained event does not by itself identify its cause or authenticate a religion. Scripture warns that impressive signs can accompany deception.

prompt.text: Could we distinguish the possibility of God's action from the evidence for this particular report?
